extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent applicants, inventors, and attorneys preparing patent application abstracts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting the abstract (abstract of disclosure) for a U.S. non‑provisional patent application, covering required formatting, content limits, common pitfalls, and best practices to improve clarity and avoid USPTO objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate sheet and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract must be included in the application on its own sheet of paper proceeding the claim section and must be clearly labeled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the USPTO outline for patent abstracts; failure to put the abstract on a separate sheet can trigger USPTO objections or require correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word limit (≤150 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract must consist of 150 words or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the abstract under the 150‑word ceiling required by the USPTO. Exceeding the limit is a common reason for office action or rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient length (avoid being too short)
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should not be overly short; abstracts that are too short (fewer than 50 words) can be inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being too brief may make the invention unclear and can draw objections. Strike a balance between brevity and sufficient description of the invention's essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey basic idea and nature of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract must clearly give the basic idea and nature of the invention disclosed in the technical part of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the invention's essence so examiners, the public, and courts can quickly understand what the application is about without reading the full specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single paragraph format
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent abstract should not be longer than one paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the abstract to one paragraph to meet USPTO expectations and improve readability; a single paragraph helps ensure conciseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claims and legal scope language
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts do not need to mention claims or their scope. This isn't the legal part of the application, so leave that topic out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include claim language or attempt to define legal scope in the abstract — claims belong in the claims section and including them can be improper or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid promotional/comparative language
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts should avoid claims, legal jargon, comparisons, or marketing language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid words like “revolutionary” or “novel” and do not compare the invention to prior inventions or marketability — those belong elsewhere in the application or prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly technical or legal jargon; use plain language
rubrics_metrics.description: Use plain language. Patent abstracts shouldn't use too much legal jargon. Leave the legal language for the claims section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write so that someone with a basic understanding of patents can grasp the invention; clear non‑expert language improves searchability and usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start directly with function or structure (avoid leading phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should avoid leading phrases like “This abstract describes…”. The abstract should start directly with the invention’s function or structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin the abstract by stating what the invention is or does rather than prefatory boilerplate; leading phrases are unnecessary and discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the core contribution
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and communicate the central technical advance or purpose rather than peripheral details; emphasize what is new or useful about the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify purpose and key features
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the invention’s purpose and key features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the invention’s purpose and main structural or functional elements that embody that purpose, so readers can quickly grasp its essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight utility (how it solves a problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight utility. Emphasize how the invention solves a problem or improves existing solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the practical benefit or improvement the invention provides — this aids public notice and can improve licensing interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid redundancy and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid redundancy. Do not repeat the title or claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restate the title or duplicate claim wording in the abstract; redundant text wastes words and may reduce clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity for non-experts while remaining precise
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective abstract strikes a balance—clear enough to be understood by non-experts but precise enough to reflect the essence of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for language accessible to a general technical audience while ensuring the abstract accurately reflects the invention’s technical contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not summarize an abstract idea only (patent eligibility awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract must summarize a practical, concrete invention; abstract ideas themselves are not patentable under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid framing the invention solely as an abstract idea (e.g., pure math or generic business practice). Where relevant, tie the idea to a specific, practical application to avoid eligibility issues (see Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank).

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow MPEP/USPTO guidelines and outline
rubrics_metrics.description: As an applicant is preparing his documents to apply for a patent for his invention, he should reference the Manual of Patent Examination Procedure rules and specifications to be sure that he is handling everything properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the USPTO/MPEP outline for abstracts to ensure formal compliance with formatting and content rules and reduce risk of office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common USPTO objection reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: There are a handful of reasons why an abstract could be rejected by the USPTO: not on a separate sheet, too short (<50) or over the 150‑word limit, inappropriate language, or failure to describe the invention properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the listed potential objections and address them proactively when drafting; correcting such issues can otherwise delay examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer or attorney review before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing USPTO guidelines and having a colleague or attorney review your draft can ensure compliance and readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A second pair of eyes helps trim excess, catch compliance issues, and improve clarity; consider attorney review to avoid procedural or substantive errors.
